scenario: AITA for telling people there is no end credit scene? | IF YOU CARE ABOUT END CREDIT SCENES LIKE THESE PEOPLE DONT READ I GUESS So, I have been working at a movie theater for a summer job, and my movie theater has ushers, but ushers at our theater don’t rip people’s tickets, they just clean the theaters. So that’s what I’ve been doing recently on my shifts and it’s pretty laid back and easy. So ushers get a door sheet, and it has what theaters to go to in an order so you can clean each theater after everyone gets out efficiently. And I had Dark Phoenix and another movie to clean at the same time. It’s super slow on weekdays so it’s not a big deal. But I knew the other movie besides Dark Phoenix was pretty crowded so I wanted to be as efficient as possible. So when I walked into Dark Phoenix, and the credits were rolling, there was 4 sets of people still in the theater presumably waiting for the end credit scene like most super hero movies have these days. So, to help them out (in my mind I guess) and myself out to clean the theater faster, I told them “hey guys, you don’t have to wait around there’s no end credit scene.” I’ve done this many times with no issues but this couple in this showing had an issue. They got up from their seat and yelled at me for “ruining their movie going experience” and wanted to speak to a manager. So I call a manger to the theater and they tell the manger that I was rude for spoiling that there was no end credit scene and they complained also that I was shining a flash light as well. I told my manager that last part was false but I didn’t see an issue with telling them as it saved them time. My manager told the couple we were sorry and he gave them a free movie pass. Once they left, my manager told me to just stop telling people about how there’s no end credit scene. So Reddit, AITA for telling people there’s no end credit scene or was this just a weird couple?

Clean & Prepare the House (Most Critical First!)** - **Deep clean** high-traffic areas (living room, kitchen, guest rooms). - **Declutter** surfaces, floors, and entryways for a welcoming vibe. - **Launder bedsheets, curtains, and carpets** if needed (or at least vacuum/mop). - **Replace air filters** (if AC/heaters are running) for fresh air. ### **2. Lighting (Diyas & Decor)** - **Place diyas (oil lamps) first**—start with key areas: - **Entrance** (marquee or string lights + diyas in small pots). - **Living room** (center table, shelves, or windowsills). - **Kitchen** (if open to guests) and **puja room** (if applicable). - **Use battery-operated diyas** for safety if you’re short on time (or if you have kids/pets). - **Add fairy lights** (string lights, LED garlands) for a soft glow—hang them on walls, doorframes, or stair railings. ### **3. Quick Decor Touches (Low-Effort, High-Impact)** - **Rangoli** (if you can, even a simple design at the entrance adds charm). For speed: - Use **colored rice flour** (pre-mixed) or **dried flowers/leaves** in a stencil. - Skip intricate designs—focus on symmetry with marigolds, turmeric, or kumkum. - **Mango leaves** (hang or place on walls/doors for auspiciousness). - **Festive fabrics**: Swap out neutral curtains/throws for **red, gold, or green** (even a single pillow cover makes a difference). - **Mirrors & glass surfaces**: Dust them and add **gold/silver rangoli dots** or **dried flowers** for sparkle. ### **4. Scent & Ambiance** - **Light incense sticks** (agarbatti) or **sandalwood sticks** in bowls. - **Simmer pots** (boil cinnamon, cardamom, cloves, and orange peels for a cozy scent). - **Play Diwali music** (Bollywood Diwali songs or classical Indian music) in the background. ### **5. Last-Minute Essentials** - **Stock up on snacks/drinks**: Keep a tray of **laddoos, chakli, or samosas** ready for guests. - **Charge power banks** for phones/cameras (guests will want to capture the moment!). - **Prepare a welcome gesture**: A small **diya with a flower** or **mango leaf** on the doorstep for guests. ### **6. Day Before Diwali** - **Test all lights/diyas** (replace batteries if needed). - **Set out guest towels/soap** in bathrooms. - **Plan a quick photo spot** (e.g., a decorated corner with diyas and rangoli). ### **Time-Saving Tips:** - **Delegate**: Ask a family member to handle one area (e.g., "You handle the kitchen diyas, I’ll do the living room"). - **Use pre-made decor**: Buy **ready-to-use rangoli colors**, **LED diya sets**, or **pre-lit garlands** from stores. - **Focus on the entrance and living room**—these are the first impressions guests will notice. ### **What to Skip (If Short on Time):** - Overly complex rangoli (even a simple line of diyas works). - Heavy, bulky decor (opt for lightweight items like fairy lights). - Perfuming the entire house (a few incense sticks or a simmer pot suffice). ### **Final Checklist (Night Before):** - [ ] All diyas are lit (or batteries charged). - [ ] Rangoli is set (even if minimal). - [ ] Entrance is welcoming (lights, mango leaves, small diya). - [ ] Snacks/drinks are ready. - [ ] Music is playing (optional but festive!). You’ve got this! This was a **separate issue** from the end credit comment. 4. **Workplace Policy Matters** - Your manager explicitly told you to stop doing this, which means: - The theater **doesn’t want ushers spoiling post-credits scenes** (likely because it’s seen as bad customer service). - The couple’s complaint was valid enough to warrant a **manager’s intervention and a free pass**—a significant escalation for the theater. - Even if you *think* you’re helping, **following company policy is non-negotiable** in a job. You’re not the first usher to get yelled at for this, and you likely won’t be the last. - **The free pass was a reasonable compromise** for the theater. It’s a small cost to avoid bad PR or repeat complaints. - **Their perspective was valid**: They paid to see a movie, and part of the experience was the post-credits scene. You **ruined that** by cutting it short. --- ### **What Would Be the Right Approach?** If you *had* to intervene (e.g., for cleaning), here’s how to do it **without ruining the experience**: 1. **Verify First**: Check if the movie has a post-credits scene before assuming. 2. **Give a Warning**: *"Hey, this one doesn’t have a post-credits scene—you might want to leave now if you’re waiting for it!"* (This lets them decide.) 3. **Avoid Flashlights**: If you need to clean, use **soft lighting** or wait until the theater is empty. 4. **Follow Company Policy**: If your manager says to stop, stop. It’s not about "being right"; it’s about **not creating unnecessary conflict**. --- ### **Final Verdict: 0/1 (Mostly Wrong)** - **You were wrong** because: - You **assumed** there was no post-credits scene without verifying. - You **disrupted a shared experience** without offering an alternative. - You **ignored company policy**, which led to a complaint and a managerial reprimand. - **You weren’t entirely wrong** because: - Some movies *do* lack post-credits scenes, and efficiency matters. - The couple’s reaction was **overly dramatic** (but still valid in context). **Lesson Learned**: In customer-facing jobs, **default to kindness and transparency**—even if it means taking a few extra minutes. Theaters rely on repeat customers, and ruining someone’s movie experience (even unintentionally) can backfire. --- ### **Bonus: How to Handle This Next Time (If It Happens Again)** If you’re ever in a similar situation: 1. **Don’t assume**—check the movie’s credits online. 2. **Use a subtle cue**: *"The credits are rolling—you might want to head out if you’re waiting for something after!"* 3. **Prioritize the audience**: If people are clearly waiting, let them stay (even if it slows you down slightly). 4. **Document the issue**: If you’re wrongly accused (like with the flashlight), **politely correct the record** with your manager afterward.
